lessons.title: Grades, classes and defects
lessons.html:
What is grading?

Grading means sorting fruit into quality classes according to a standard. Graders stand along the line after washing and waxing and look at each fruit. They decide whether it is good enough for the top export class, a lower class, the local market, or juice.

Classes

The exact names and rules depend on the fruit kind and the market, and are given to you by the packhouse. A common system is:

ClassDescription
Class 1 (Extra or Export top)Very good quality; only very slight blemishes allowed
Class 2Good quality; some small defects allowed
Class 3 / local marketSound fruit with more visible defects
Juice / processingSound fruit not good enough for fresh market
WasteRotten or seriously damaged fruit

Common defects

  • Blemishes: wind scars, scratches, thrips or mite marks, spray marks.
  • Bruises: soft, discoloured areas from knocks or pressure.
  • Sunburn: yellow, brown or bleached patches.
  • Hail damage: dents or healed marks.
  • Insect damage: holes, stings or scale insects.
  • Misshapen fruit: not the typical shape of the cultivar.
  • Off-colour: not the colour required for that class.
  • Decay: mould, soft rot or leaking fruit.
  • Skin breaks: cuts, punctures and splits that let rot in.

For many defects the size of the defect matters. A tiny healed scar may be allowed in Class 1, while a larger one moves the fruit down a class. Learn the defect limits from the grading chart and photos.

lessons.title: Grading on the line
lessons.html:
Before grading starts

  1. Get the grading instructions for the batch: fruit, cultivar, market, and which classes are being packed.
  2. Look at the defect chart or reference photos for this market.
  3. Wash your hands and put on your apron and hairnet.
  4. Check your station: lights working, bins or lanes for each class correctly marked.

How to grade

  • Watch the fruit as it rotates on the rollers so you see all sides.
  • Work on your section of the line. Do not reach far across.
  • When you see a defect, judge how serious it is according to the standard.
  • Move the fruit gently to the correct lane, belt or bin. Do not throw it.
  • Pick out decayed fruit first; it can spread to others.
  • Be consistent: grade every fruit by the same rules, all day.

Stay focused

Grading needs good eyes and concentration. Tiredness causes mistakes. Use your breaks, rotate positions if your packhouse does this, and tell your supervisor if the line is too fast or the lights are poor. If you see many fruit with the same defect, report it; it may show a problem in the orchard or on the line, such as a sharp edge causing cuts.

Checking your grading

Quality controllers take samples from each class and check them against the standard. They count how many fruit have defects that should not be in that class. If too many are wrong, the class fails and fruit may need to be re-graded. Listen to feedback from QCs; it helps you improve.

Hygiene and safety

Never eat on the line, wash your hands after handling rotten fruit, keep hands out of moving rollers and know the emergency stop. Stand on the mat and keep good posture.

Key points

  • Grading sorts fruit into quality classes according to the market standard.
  • Know the common defects and their size limits for each class.
  • Look at all sides of the fruit and handle it gently.
  • Remove decayed fruit first and grade consistently.
  • Report repeated defects and use QC feedback to improve.
